Anthropic revenue jumps to US$16.8 billion in Q3 before IPO
SAN FRANCISCO - Anthropic told prospective investors its third-quarter revenue hit US$16.8 billion (S$21.6 billion), according to people familiar with the matter, as the artificial intelligence model maker pushes ahead with plans to go public.
The firm behind Claude told investors it had achieved profitability in the quarter on an adjusted basis in a presentation on Oct 14 at its San Francisco headquarters, the people said.
Anthropic is set to begin formally marketing for its initial public offering as soon as the week of Nov 9, putting it in line to begin trading before Thanksgiving, Bloomberg News has reported. Anthropic is expected to make its debut no later than the end of the year.
Deliberations are ongoing and the timeline could continue to shift, the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public. The Financial Times reported some of the figures earlier on Oct 14. A spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment.
Anthropic, ascendant for much of this year, now faces renewed competition from the likes of OpenAI, which is neck and neck with its rival in the race for a higher valuation. The companies are also at the center of mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents, ramping up concern about the potential impact on Anthropic’s IPO.
Meta Platforms Inc. added to competitors for investors to monitor after releasing an AI model which the company says is a big leap over its own predecessors. Muse Wonder’s capabilities put it on par with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude when it comes to coding, or working through financial or legal questions, according to the company.
Investors’ reactions to Anthropic’s update will be critical to the IPO process, with some indicating prior to the Oct 14 meeting that a fair valuation for the company is in the US$1.8 trillion to US$2 trillion ballpark. The company expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s IPO, Bloomberg News has reported.
Anthropic had a net loss of almost US$42 billion in 2025, a roughly fivefold increase from about US$8.3 billion the year before, Bloomberg News reported in August. The company’s full-year revenue was roughly US$4.6 billion for 2025, up markedly from US$386 million in the year before, though its operating loss ballooned to more than US$8 billion, according to documents seen by Bloomberg News.
Powering ahead with an IPO would see Anthropic defy a string of delays and postponements in the market for new listings globally.
Data centre operator AirTrunk delayed the IPO of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027, days after a planned IPO for Australian data centre company Firmus collapsed. BLOOMBERG

indian-startups-621a275259.headline: Jio Platforms Sets Stage For India’s Largest IPO At ₹10.3 Lakh Cr Valuation
indian-startups-621a275259.fulltext: Telecom giant Jio Platforms has set a price band of ₹1,065-₹1,119 per share for its IPO, which is set to open for public subscription next week. The company is seeking to raise ₹30,213 Cr at the upper end of the price band, overtaking Hyundai Motor’s ₹27,870 Cr IPO in 2024 to become the largest public offering to hit the Indian equities market till date. At the upper end of the IPO, RIL’s telecom arm is seeking a valuation of ₹10.3 Lakh Cr for the IPO. Jio filed its red herring prospectus (RHP) earlier today for its IPO comprising a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares. Post anchor bidding on October 19 (Monday), the IPO will open for public subscription on October 21 and close on October 23. The telco has reserved ₹500 Cr worth shares for eligible employees, who can avail a discount of ₹54 per share. Additionally, up to ₹2,500 Cr will be reserved for eligible shareholders of RIL. The company intends to utilise ₹27,500 Cr of the fresh capital raised via the IPO for prepayment, in full or in part, of certain outstanding borrowings availed by its material subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL). The remaining proceeds, ₹2,713 Cr to be precise, will be allocated for general corporate purposes may fund strategic initiatives, growth opportunities, capital expenditure, working capital, marketing and other business requirements. The issue has no OFS component, meaning existing shareholders will not sell shares through the IPO. RIL currently holds a 66.43% stake in Jio Platforms, while Meta and Google own 9.98% and 7.73%, respectively.

world-d96a844684.headline: Ukrainian military’s access to Starlink satellite internet suddenly restricted
world-d96a844684.fulltext:
Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.
The terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.
Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force. But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.
Musk said that Starlink is not licensed to clients who are using weapons, and that the Ukrainian military was linked to a separate network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government. “This is not under SpaceX control,” Musk wrote.
Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals has been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected. The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.
Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader – an extraordinary act of political interference against a wartime ally – as a personal feud between the two presidents has burst into the open.
The reports that Starlink was being throttled on the frontlines were interpreted by some as further pressure on Ukraine to end the fighting and make a deal with Russia at any cost.
Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”
Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” Zelenskyy said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed by either side. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”
Ukraine is observing a short-term moratorium on striking Russian refineries while Kyiv seeks to show that it is ready for talks with Russia. Zelenskyy arrived in London on Wednesday to meet Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister. He will also be received by King Charles.
Zelenskyy is seeking new negotiations with the US. He has sent proposals to the Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, saying Ukraine was ready to work towards a ceasefire and “Russia must also be part of this agreement”.

india-deep-tech-14c238cc37.headline: DRDO tests 'quantum lock' for weapon-trial data at Odisha's Chandipur
india-deep-tech-14c238cc37.fulltext:
India
DRDO tests 'quantum lock' for weapon-trial data at Odisha's Chandipur
The platform tested on live military network secures real-time data from artillery and armoured trials.
NEW DELHI: Quantum encryption has moved from field trials to a live military network. The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has tested its Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) platform on the operational network of its Chandipur test ranges in Odisha, securing real-time data from artillery and armoured weapon trials.
In a statement on X on Wednesday, DRDO said it had "successfully configured and tested a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) platform in the live network of the dynamic test ranges at Proof & Experimental Establishment (PXE), Chandipur."
"This demonstrates the adept use case of QKD to fortify the real-time critical observations & telemetry associated with Artillery and Armoured Weapon tests and evaluation," it added.
Telemetry is the stream of readings beamed back by sensors during a test, such as a shell's speed, trajectory and point of impact. This data reveals how a weapon performs, which makes it a prime target for spies.
So how does QKD work? Every encrypted message needs a secret "key" to lock and unlock it. The fresh test’s encryption protects that key with complex mathematical puzzles, which future quantum computers could crack.
QKD instead sends the key as tiny particles of light, called photons, over optical fibre. Under the laws of quantum physics, merely observing these particles disturbs them. So any attempt to tap the line is instantly detected, much like a seal that breaks the moment anyone peeks.
The QKD system "has been designed and developed under Microelectronic Devices, Computational Systems & Cyber Security (MCC) cluster of DRDO with production partner Taqbit labs and will aptly provide unconditional security added with eavesdropping detection," DRDO said. A"Unconditional" means the security does not depend on how powerful an attacker's computer is.
The Chandipur test caps a series of steps. In February 2022, DRDO and IIT-Delhi scientists demonstrated a QKD link of over 100 km between Prayagraj and Vindhyachal in Uttar Pradesh, a first for the country.
In June last year, they sent quantum keys through open air, without any cable, over more than one km on the IIT-Delhi campus. Such "free-space" links could one day secure communications on battlefields, aircraft and satellites, where laying fibre is impractical.
Then, in July this year, DRDO and Bengaluru-based Taqbit Labs, which has worked with it since 2020, completed military field trials of a scalable, fibre-based QKD system.
PXE's range at Chandipur runs 50 km along the coast and 50 km into the sea. Artillery shells, rockets and armour protection are put through their paces there.
The push comes amid a global race to "quantum-proof" military networks. India's Rs 6,003-crore National Quantum Mission aims for satellite-based secure quantum links over 2,000 km by 2030-31.
The New Indian Express

deep-tech-49b61843b7.headline: Reflect Orbital Buys Two Skyroot Aerospace Launches
deep-tech-49b61843b7.fulltext:
Reflect Orbital, the startup attempting to offer sunlight on-demand with in-space mirrors, announced the purchase of two launches today from Indian launcher Skyroot Aerospace.
The deal includes:
- One launch on Skyroot’s Vikram-1 launch vehicle, which debuted in July, and can carry ~350kg to LEO.
- One launch on Skyroot’s upgraded Vikram-1U vehicle, which is expected to fly its first mission in Q1 2027, and will be capable of carrying ~550kg to LEO.
Reflect Orbital did not disclose the cost of each launch, or when the missions would fly.
Precious inventory: The deal comes amid a launch capacity crisis that has forced some operators to buy their own dedicated vehicles, as SpaceX has stopped accepting reservations after 2029 for its popular Transporter rideshare program.
Despite that, companies are still finding ways to get to orbit. For example, in August, Portal Space Systems announced it purchased a full SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for Portal’s Motus Via Sol mission in 2028. Portal doesn’t expect to fill the Falcon 9 to the brim, however, and made a deal with Maverick Space Systems who later filled most of the available space with 10 Kepler satellites.
A spokesperson from Reflect Orbital told Payload the company “is the primary and only payload at this time.”
Blinding lights: In July, Reflect Orbital received FCC approval to fly its first in-space mirror-satellite—Eärendil-1—but the company’s larger plan is to fly a constellation of ~50,000 mirrors to provide sunlight on Earth after dark.
The idea is to use the constellation to provide extra sunlight for terrestrial solar farms to generate power after sunset, but the company also plans to provide sunlight for everything from search-and-rescue operations, to nighttime concerts.

ai-42168fd35c.headline: Eight states accuse OpenAI of coaching children to harm themselves in lawsuit
ai-42168fd35c.fulltext:
Eight US states sued OpenAI Wednesday, alleging the ChatGPT maker is harming children en masse.
Kansas, Arizona, Montana, Iowa and four others allege the company’s products carried out “willful, dangerous, reckless and unlawful conduct” by coaxing children into harming themselves.
“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Brenna Bird, the attorney general for Iowa, said in a statement. “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide – all while pretending to be their fake friend.”
All eight states accuse OpenAI of violating consumer protection laws and seek to force the company to change how its products work for young users. They are additionally seeking monetary damages, and asking the court to halt OpenAI from developing artificial intelligence models that can improve upon themselves until the company shows those models are in line with human values.
This is the first time several US states have banded together in a coordinated legal action against an AI company.
Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company had “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack”.
“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” Pusateri continued. “We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company.”
The lawsuits allege that OpenAI has been misleading the public into believing that ChatGPT is a safe tool and that the company puts safety first. The states say that in reality, the chatbot has been designed to be “overly agreeable and feign human compassion”. The attorneys point to examples of ChatGPT being dangerous to vulnerable users, like children, and coaching people to commit suicide or harm others.
This comes after a groundswell of cases have been brought against OpenAI and other tech companies alleging that their chatbots exacerbate mental health crises and provoke violent acts. OpenAI has been sued in seven separate cases that blame ChatGPT for acting as a “suicide coach”.
Dozens of cases have also been filed against OpenAI over ChatGPT’s alleged role in mass shootings. A criminal investigation and civil lawsuit, brought by the attorney general of Florida, accuses OpenAI of concealing safety risks after a mass shooting at Florida State University. The company has also been sued by the families of 37 victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in Canada, who allege ChatGPT induced the shooter to carry out the attack.
The eight states that filed suit on Wednesday say there is a growing body of research that allegedly shows ChatGPT can harm critical-thinking skills, encourage paranoia and delusions, offer dangerous medical advice and promote unhealthy behavior.
The lawsuits also note that the recent examples of OpenAI’s models going rogue, with its AI agents hacking into other companies and government entities, show that the technology is prone to deceiving human users.
Pusateri said OpenAI had strengthened its safeguards in regards to those episodes and would “continue sharing information about the extensive steps we’ve taken in response to incidents of misalignment”.
The eight states are suing OpenAI independently in their state courts and include Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana.

india-84572a6558.headline: India, U.S. ironing out differences on trade deal; nearing 'landing point': Jaishankar
india-84572a6558.fulltext:
India and the U.S. are continuing to engage to iron out differences on the proposed trade deal, and negotiations are heading towards a "landing point," External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has said, while noting that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remain unchanged.
The External Affairs Minister's comments on the trade negotiations came over a week after Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks on the trade deal have reached a "plateau".
"I think we are waiting on a few things. I wouldn't be comfortable spilling the beans in public," he said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum on Tuesday evening when asked about the status of the negotiations between the two sides.
Mr. Jaishankar said India's trade minister, the US Trade Representative (USTR) and other officials concerned are engaged in talks to move forward on the bilateral trade pact.
"When countries negotiate with an economy like the United States, obviously one part of it is what you work out between yourselves and the U.S., and one part of it is how do you fare vis-a-vis competitive economies.
"And that part of it is not entirely clear because not everybody has worked out a deal. I think people, the trade ministers, USTR (U.S. Trade Representative), and our Commerce and Industry Minister are there working on that. They're ironing it out," he said.
"My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point," Mr. Jaishankar said.
India and the U.S. have been in talks since early 2025 on the proposed trade pact to address tariff friction, eliminate non-tariff barriers, and boost bilateral market access.
India is seeking better tariffs than its competitors for its goods in the U.S. market.
Earlier this month, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the United States and India were working to finalise a bilateral trade deal, but an agreement was not imminent.
Mr. Greer said the two sides identified the issues that remained unresolved and were working towards an agreement.
In his remarks, Mr. Jaishankar also delved into Washington's new approach on economic engagement.
"The U.S. has a fundamentally different approach to the use of tariffs. But even that is a symptom of something else. The US is today determined to re-industrialise and to reset the terms of access to its economy," he said.
"That's what the whole tariff debate is about. And the two are connected: access to the American economy and the re-industrialisation of America. Therefore, what is happening is every significant economy is getting into a negotiation with the United States on this issue," he said.
"We're not alone in this. In our case, we are pretty far advanced in that process of negotiation," he said.
Mr. Jaishankar also noted that the U.S. is revising the terms of its alliances and treaty relationships and that the sentiment is most strongly being felt in Europe, and to some extent, in some countries in East Asia.
"We have many issues we are working on with the United States, but we don't have an issue of the terms of alliance because we are not officially an ally. We are a country which has a strong strategic partnership with the US, but a strategic partnership is a partnership; it's not an alliance," he added.
"In our case, for the last 20-odd years, we have worked out what we felt were convergences, overlaps, shared common interests with the US, and we had agreed that we would pursue that. I don't think that has fundamentally changed," he said.
The India-U.S. relations witnessed a major downturn after Washington imposed punitive tariffs on India last year and President Donald Trump made assertions regarding his role in de-escalating the India-Pakistan military clashes of May 2025 that drew sharp reaction from Indian officials.
Washington's new immigration policy and its decision to increase H1B visa fee also contributed to the slide in India-U.S. ties.
The ties came under fresh strain after the US decided to restrict a key green-card processing programme for major global and Indian IT firms, including Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro.

ai-ca567069ec.headline: Scimplify raises $25M to challenge China’s grip on critical materials with AI
ai-ca567069ec.fulltext:
As manufacturers across industries strive to reduce their reliance on Chinese suppliers, Indian startup Scimplify has raised $25 million to expand its AI-powered approach to producing specialty chemicals and critical materials, with semiconductors, defense, and energy emerging as key growth markets.
The all-equity strategic round was led by Hitachi Ventures, with customers Henkel and Teknor Apex joining as new investors. Existing backers Accel India, Bertelsmann India Investments, Omnivore, and 3one4 Capital also participated. The round values the Bengaluru-based startup at $250 million after the investment, according to a person familiar with the transaction, up from $150 million after a $40 million Series B round in March 2025. The latest investment brings Scimplify’s total equity funding to $80 million, the startup said, though it declined to disclose its valuation.
The growing adoption of AI and advanced computational tools has accelerated materials discovery and research. However, turning promising chemistry into commercially available products at scale remains a slow and complex process. Manufacturers need to develop production processes, qualify facilities, and meet stringent quality standards, all while navigating supply chains limited to a handful of countries. Scimplify is seeking to shorten that process.
In some cases, the startup, founded in 2023, has gone from receiving a customer’s requirements to delivering the finished material in just two months, compared with the 12 to 18 months such work would typically take, co-founder Sachin Santhosh (pictured above) said in an interview.
Once it receives an order, Scimplify develops chemical manufacturing processes at its research facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad and then transfers them to partner factories for commercial production. Its proprietary AI platform, Scinode, helps coordinate the work by identifying suitable production routes and manufacturing facilities, while tracking quality and regulatory requirements. The platform uses specialized AI agents for different functions, including research, manufacturing, and quality control, Santhosh told TechCrunch.
“Each of these agents is basically solving for what [a customer] would want, working backward from the customer’s requirement,” Santhosh said. “This helps us move a lot faster and remember customer context even for future references.”
Scimplify’s in-house team of scientists and engineers oversees production across a network of more than 500 manufacturing facilities. It helps customers establish alternative sources for materials whose supply is concentrated in China and a few other countries.
About 90% of Scimplify’s manufacturing currently takes place in India. The startup, however, plans to expand its production network to the U.S. and Japan over the next year as it seeks to attract more customers in both markets, Santhosh said.
The U.S. has emerged as a key growth market, with Scimplify’s annualized revenue run rate in the country rising sixfold to about $60 million from $10 million a year ago, according to Santhosh. The market now accounts for roughly 30% of its business, while customers outside India collectively contribute more than half of its revenue, compared with less than 5% about 18 months ago.
Overall, Scimplify, which serves more than 1,000 customers and has delivered products to more than 40 countries, has reached an annualized revenue run rate of about $200 million, tripling from a year earlier, Santhosh told TechCrunch. The startup is targeting a $400 million annualized revenue run rate over the next year. Scimplify has also been EBITDA-positive for the past two months and expects to turn profitable after tax this month, he said.
Energy, electronics, and defense now account for about 45% to 50% of Scimplify’s revenue, up from less than 15% a year ago, Santhosh stated. The growth comes as AI fuels demand for materials used in electronics and energy infrastructure, while ongoing wars drive demand from the defense industry.
Scimplify is working on producing tungsten derivatives from scrap, offering customers an alternative source of materials whose supply is heavily concentrated in China. The startup is also working on rare-earth materials, another category where global supply chains remain heavily dependent on China.
The startup works with customers including Japanese electronics manufacturer TDK, German chemicals group BASF, and Hitachi. Santhosh cited a project involving TDK as an example of how the startup can shorten the time needed to develop and deliver specialty materials. Timelines, he said, vary depending on the project.
With its latest funding, Scimplify plans to deploy around $7.5 million for its U.S. expansion, including building out its manufacturing network, Santhosh said, adding that the allocation could change as the startup’s plans evolve. It also earmarked another $2 million for further development of Scinode.
The startup employs about 340 people, including roughly 70 scientists. Most of its workforce is based in India, though it also has local teams in the U.S., Japan, Indonesia, and the UAE.

China’s integrated circuit (IC) exports surged 136 per cent year on year in September to US$45 billion, exceeding the 108 per cent growth rate in the first nine months of the year in a sign of the country’s rising influence in the global semiconductor supply chain.
In September, China exported 32.7 billion units of ICs, according to customs data released on Wednesday, a 1 per cent year-on-year increase in volume. But higher prices fuelled the 136 per cent jump in value amid a memory chip shortage stemming from the global building spree in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The first three quarters as a whole saw exports of 275.2 billion IC units worth nearly US$302 billion, according to the General Administration of Customs.
The growth in semiconductor exports far outpaced overall export growth from China, which rose 36.3 per cent year on year to US$447.18 billion last month.
The data shows how Chinese chipmakers remain deeply entrenched in the global tech supply chain despite not producing the most advanced hardware given their limited access to top-of-the-line manufacturing equipment.
“The booming development of AI has accelerated global investment in computing power, expanding the demand for terminal equipment and intermediate manufacturing products,” said Wang Jun, spokesman and vice-minister of the customs authority, in a news briefing on Wednesday.
The operation of massive computing facilities has simultaneously driven up global demand for electricity equipment, prompting a surge in Chinese power-related exports across generation, transmission and energy storage, he added.
Beyond chips, other hardware products also saw higher shipments. Exports of computer parts grew 2.1 times year on year during the nine-month period, exports of memory components like solid-state drives increased 1.3 times and exports of data-processing equipment – such as servers – rose by 7.2 per cent, Wang said.
Chinese-made AI glasses and robots are also continuously entering international markets as they “enrich global AI application scenarios”, Wang said, without disclosing exact trade figures.
Meanwhile, semiconductor imports have also been growing quickly owing to China’s heavy investment in digital and AI infrastructure. Memory imports grew 150 per cent year on year in the first nine months of the year, while IC imports rose 56.6 per cent, Wang said.

- Manipal Academy of Higher Education launched Manipal House of Quantum, Quantum-Hub@MAHE, at MIT Bengaluru to support quantum engineering, hardware experimentation and indigenous technology development in India.
- The facility begins operations with a 25-qubit open-architecture dilution refrigeration system, with plans to progress toward 150-qubit proof-of-concept platforms and industrial systems exceeding 1,000 qubits.

PRESS RELEASE — Manipal Institute of Technology, Bengaluru (MIT Bengaluru) on Tuesday launched Manipal House of Quantum, Quantum-Hub@MAHE. Established by Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE), an Institution of Eminence Deemed to be University, the initiative will advance quantum hardware experimentation, engineering education and indigenous technology development in alignment with India’s National Quantum Mission.
The facility was inaugurated by Chief Guest Dr. Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist & Co-Founder, Zoho Corp, and Guest of Honour Dr. Marcus Rommel, CTO, ConScience, in the presence of Dr. Sharath K. Rao, Vice Chancellor, MAHE; Lieutenant General (Dr.) M. D. Venkatesh, VSM (Retd.), 7th Vice Chancellor, MAHE and Advisor to MEMG; Prof. (Dr.) Madhu Veeraraghavan, Pro Vice Chancellor, MAHE Bengaluru; Dr. Karunakar A. Kotegar, Pro Vice Chancellor, Technology & Science, MAHE; Dr. Raghavendra Prabhu, Additional Registrar, MAHE Bengaluru; Prof. Iven Jose, Director, MIT Bengaluru; and Mr. Vishal Chatrath, Co-Founder & CEO, QuantrolOX.
Located at the MAHE Bengaluru campus, the quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru provides students, researchers and industry collaborators with hands-on access to advanced quantum computing infrastructure, including quantum hardware, cryogenic systems and quantum control technologies. Through an integrated academic framework, the facility will support experimentation, application development, deep-tech start-up incubation, component innovation, testing and translational research, positioning MIT Bengaluru as an emerging centre for quantum engineering and indigenous hardware development.
The facility commences operations with a 25-qubit open-architecture dilution refrigeration system designed for advanced training and experimentation. This marks the first phase of a structured roadmap progressing from sub-50-qubit training systems to 150-qubit proof-of-concept platforms and, ultimately, to industrial-grade quantum product systems with more than 1,000 qubits.
Speaking at the inauguration, Dr. Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist & Co-Founder, Zoho Corp, said, “Q-HUB is a place for students to dream, think deeply and turn their ideas into conviction and action. Just as personal computers and the internet transformed possibilities for my generation, quantum computing can empower this generation to build new machines, create breakthrough applications and take India to greater heights.”
Highlighting MAHE’s commitment to emerging technologies, Dr. Sharath K. Rao, Vice Chancellor, MAHE, said, “The MAHE House of Quantum at MIT Bengaluru reflects MAHE’s commitment to building advanced scientific capabilities and nurturing talent in emerging technologies. By creating access to modern quantum infrastructure, we aim to contribute meaningfully to India’s growing quantum ecosystem.”
Prof. (Dr.) Madhu Veeraraghavan, Pro Vice Chancellor, MAHE Bengaluru, said, “The Hub brings together education, research and innovation on a common platform. It will create opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration and help translate academic research into real-world technological impact.”
Prof. Iven Jose, Director, MIT Bengaluru, said, “The quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru will provide students and researchers with valuable exposure to real quantum systems and engineering environments. It marks an important step towards developing the next generation of quantum scientists, engineers and innovators.”
Ahead of the launch, faculty members and students from the Bengaluru and Manipal campuses completed specialised training at the MIT Bengaluru campus and the QuantrolOx laboratory at QuTech, TU Delft, in the Netherlands. The programme developed practical capabilities in dilution refrigerator assembly, cryogenic systems, quantum control technologies, QPU measurements and superconducting quantum hardware, preparing the team to support the operations of the quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru.
The facility will support learning and research in areas such as healthcare, pharmaceuticals, oncology, aerospace and advanced computing. It will also strengthen MIT Bengaluru’s collaboration with industry and research organisations while developing a future-ready talent pipeline in quantum technologies.
The initiative has been formalised through Memorandums of Agreement with QuantrolOx of Finland, in association with Bluefors of Finland, Qblox of the Netherlands and ConScience of Sweden. These collaborations establish a first-year roadmap focused on workforce development, hardware experimentation, intellectual property co-development and national testing infrastructure.
As part of its workforce development efforts, the quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru aims to train 100 quantum engineers by December 2026. It will also conduct quantum awareness programmes, summer and winter camps for Class 10 and Class 12 students across rural India, short hands-on exposure programmes and capacity-building initiatives for technical professionals.
The facility will provide researchers, start-ups and industry partners with access to advanced quantum testing and measurement infrastructure, strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration, innovation and India’s growing quantum technology ecosystem.

The Technology Development Board (TDB) has signed an agreement with Mumbai-based ideaForge Technology Limited to provide ₹151 crore in debt financing for the development of YETI, an indigenous heavy-lift autonomous aerial logistics vehicle.
The support, under the Research Development and Innovation Fund, forms part of a ₹302-crore project aimed at advancing the platform from Technology Readiness Level 4 to TRL-9 through engineering, integration, testing and validation.
YETI is being developed as a hybrid vertical take-off and landing, fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle capable of carrying payloads of up to 200 kg. Its targeted range is up to 200 km, with an operating altitude of up to 6,500 metres above mean sea level.
The platform is intended to transport supplies in locations where conventional movement is difficult, time-consuming or operationally constrained. Its weather-resistant design aims to support operations in high-altitude regions, deserts and marine environments.
Combining vertical take-off and landing with fixed-wing flight, YETI is designed to operate from relatively small, unprepared landing areas measuring approximately 15 metres by 15 metres. This would allow deployment in places with limited ground infrastructure.
The proposed system includes distributed and redundant propulsion and power architecture to improve fault tolerance. Other planned capabilities include navigation without Global Navigation Satellite System signals, a communication link of up to 200 km, swarm operations and containerised transportation for rapid deployment.
The programme will support further development towards TRL-9, subject to applicable technical, safety and regulatory requirements. It falls within the deep-technology sector, under intelligent systems and robotics, integrating aerospace engineering, propulsion, navigation, communications and intelligent control.
TDB Secretary Rajesh Kumar Pathak said indigenous heavy-lift aerial platforms could improve access to remote and difficult-to-reach locations.
“Through the RDI Fund, TDB is supporting technology-intensive projects that require sustained investment to progress from advanced development towards deployment,” he said.
The agreement reflected the board’s commitment to strengthening India’s capabilities in autonomous systems, robotics and next-generation aerospace technologies, Pathak added.
IdeaForge’s CEO and co-founder described YETI as a significant step in India’s autonomous technology capabilities, designed to address the challenges faced by Armed Forces and logistics networks in areas beyond road access and under difficult weather conditions.
The company said the platform was being engineered for reliable, repeatable delivery in demanding operational environments.

The company has secured the project from the U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), a key centre of the ISRO, marking a significant step in its journey from ground-level challenges to the demands of space engineering.
As part of the contract, Genrobotics Innovations will develop a high-precision articulated boom arm system for ISRO's satellite missions, the company said in a statement here on Wednesday.

Under the URSC project, the company's Space & Advanced Robotics division will develop a multi-link articulated boom arm system designed to withstand the mechanical stresses of launch and operate under the extreme thermal and vacuum conditions of space, the statement said.
The mechanism is intended to enable precise positioning and orientation of space-borne communication reflectors and payload instruments on satellites, it said.
Besides marking a significant expansion of Genrobotics' work into advanced aerospace engineering, the project also highlights the potential of Keralam's deep-tech ecosystem to contribute to India's commercial space programme through indigenous design and manufacturing capabilities.

"Our journey began in hazardous underground manholes, where our mission was to save lives and restore human dignity," said Vimal Govind M K, co-founder and CEO of Genrobotics.

Space startups worldwide raised a record $20.8 billion in the July-September quarter, as investors poured capital into launch providers, manufacturers and other infrastructure ventures, according to a report by global investment firm Seraphim released on Wednesday (14 October).
The amount was almost three times the $7.4 billion raised in the April-June quarter and more than twice the previous high.
Even without Blue Origin’s $10 billion financing, investment touched an all-time high of $10.8 billion.
The number of deals also hit a record 216, compared with 140 in the previous quarter.

“Capital is following evidence of commercial and institutional demand, not just residual IPO enthusiasm,” said Lucas Bishop, vice president at Seraphim Space.
Infrastructure firms drew most of the money. Companies in launch and wider space access raised $16.4 billion through 120 deals, while those in satellite communications, Earth observation and other space services secured $4 billion.
Bishop said defence and sovereign demand were increasingly driving investment in launch, manufacturing and orbital infrastructure, as governments focus on building domestic space capabilities.
Among the biggest rounds of the quarter were Hadrian’s $1.37 billion, Stoke Space’s $1 billion and K2 Space’s $500 million.
Listed space firms, however, fared worse. Bishop noted that many remain loss-making and that SpaceX’s scale and visibility may have pulled investor attention away from smaller listed rivals.
North America made up nearly 70 per cent of global funding so far this year, while China posted a quarterly record of $3.3 billion across 49 deals.
Seraphim expects funding to ease from the third quarter’s exceptional level but stay above historical averages as more companies move into growth and scale-up stages.

other-interests-0535d93f80.headline: New ‘First Proof’ exam reveals how AI-powered math is a pay-to-play sport
other-interests-0535d93f80.fulltext:
Artificial intelligence models are getting good at math—but only the corporate AIs.
The First Proof project, which aims to objectively evaluate the mathematical reasoning of publicly available AI models, released its third batch of results today. They underline what recent headlines have shown—that some large language models (LLMs) are becoming powerful research tools. They also suggest that proprietary subscription-based models from so-called frontier labs far exceed the math skills of more transparent and accessible “open-weight” models.
“The gap between the open-weight models and frontier models is very large in research mathematics—much larger than in other domains,” says Mohammed Abouzaid, a mathematician at Stanford University and a member of the First Proof team.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In February a team of top mathematicians started First Proof as a rigorous, independent exam for cutting through the proliferation of imperfect “benchmarks” for scoring different models. The AI race to conquer math has accelerated dramatically since those quaint days, when its greatest successes concerned problems that were scarcely connected to actual research. OpenAI’s “slop drop” last week has put to rest scores of more pressing questions, many of which had stood unresolved for decades. And the company’s solution of the Navier-Stokes problem last month convinced many that LLMs are on the verge of superseding human mathematicians—if they have not already.
But these breakthroughs are far from controlled experiments. For the slop drop, OpenAI didn’t disclose the thousands of problems that the company’s new model attempted, most of which it didn’t solve. And that internal model remains completely inaccessible to outside mathematicians, preventing a direct comparison of its performance with others.
First Proof’s mathematicians solicited problems from experts in a broad range of subdisciplines and then selected 10. They asked each model under evaluation to answer the problems as written, with no further human input. Then they had three graders per problem evaluate the answers in a mock “peer review.”
First Proof’s rules require any entrants to be openly available, so OpenAI’s blockbuster new model was excluded. The team tested OpenAI’s GPT 6 Astra, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, an aggregate model called “ProofCouncil” that combines an Astra agent with other agents to check its work and a similar “harness” built on Kimi K3, the leading open-weight model—one whose inner workings are made completely public, among other entrants. Producers of other major models, including Google, did not participate.
The best performer—ProofCouncil—solved nine out of the 10 research problems in a manner the judges deemed acceptable with “minor revisions” for publication in a peer-reviewed journal. This helped quantify the models’ rapid ascent at math over the course of 2026. (In the round one results that First Proof released in February, the top model got just a few problems correct. And in the round two results released in June, the winner got six or seven.)
For the main skill that First Proof tests—proving well-defined statements—“the models have become very good,” Abouzaid says, “so good that testing the frontier models on this task might not be that relevant in the future.”
Notably, the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, solved exactly zero problems. “It really fell flat on its face,” says Lauren Williams, a mathematician at Harvard University and a member of the First Proof team. “The open models are really, really far behind, so we would urge the community to invest a lot into improving them.”
The First Proof team has received many requests to test open-weight models from mathematicians concerned about privacy after recent high-profile controversies. “I know people who use open-source models exclusively because they’re so paranoid about data leakage with the frontier models,” Williams says.
“We have a lot of questions from mathematicians telling us, ‘I would like to look for alternatives to using OpenAI’s or Anthropic’s models, but I don’t know whether they would work,’” Abouzaid says .
For now, it seems, they don’t.

The IPO Committee of the Board of Directors of Jio Platforms approved the price band between ₹1,065– ₹1,119 per equity share at a meeting held on Wednesday, October 14. At the upper end of the price band of ₹1,119 per share, Jio Platforms’ IPO is expected to raise around ₹30,213 crore, making it the biggest IPO in India’s stock market history. Reliance Industries’ technology arm Jio Platforms Ltd (JPL) is set to launch India’s largest-ever initial public offering (IPO) at a valuation of ₹28,755-30,213 crore, but lower than brokerage estimates that had pegged the fund raise at ₹33,000-38,000 crore. The company has filed its red herring prospectus (RHP) with the Registrar of Companies (RoC). The issue will open on October 21 and close on October 23.
The company has announced a price band of ₹1,065-1,119 per equity share, along with an employee discount of ₹54 per share for eligible employees bidding under the Employee Reservation Portion. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to 27 crore equity shares with a face value of ₹10 each.
JPL has borrowings of about ₹27,500 crore, which means the company will be left with only ₹1,255-2,713 crore from the issue proceeds for general corporate purposes and expansion plans after debt repayment. “The debt reduction is also expected to lower annual interest costs by ₹2,000-2,500 crore,” Deven Choksey, Managing Director of DRChoksey FinServ, had earlier told businessline.
“The IPO includes a reservation of equity shares of JPL worth up to ₹500 crore for eligible employees and up to ₹2,500 crore for eligible Reliance Industries shareholders, comprising individual investors and HUFs who are public shareholders of the company as of the date of the RHP filing,” Reliance said in a stock exchange filing.
The anchor investor bidding date has been fixed for October 19. The RHP does not include an offer-for-sale (OFS) component, indicating that existing investors are not looking to dilute their holdings at the time of listing. JPL’s investors include Google, Meta and Silver Lake, among others.
The IPO is expected to be India’s largest-ever public issue, surpassing previous records despite the lower-than-expected pricing. The company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹30,064 crore on revenue of ₹1.49 lakh crore in FY26.

global-economics-0241406a5c.headline: OpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annually
global-economics-0241406a5c.fulltext:
OpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.
Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.
The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings, according to the Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.
But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners. The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.
The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.
OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge. Google DeepMind is also based in King’s Cross.
The company declined to comment on the figures, which come after a series of AI safety crises involving its models. This summer AI agents, under training, escaped and hacked into an unrelated company website, Hugging Face, while this month one of its safety leaders quit, saying that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.
OpenAI’s London office has been established as its largest international research hub but it also houses a government affairs team and sales and marketing functions – responsible for selling licences to companies and organisations. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer, joined last December as the company’s head for countries.
The earnings were a big jump on the previous year, when the average pay and equity package was £1.1m.
Booming AI salaries have already had a significant effect on housing prices in San Francisco, where the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 per month, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and is nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.
In London, OpenAI UK Ltd recorded a more than trebling of its turnover in 2025 to £293m, on which it made a £20.3m profit.

The facility begins operation with a 25-qubit open-architecture dilution refrigeration system.
The new facility, established by Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE), an “Institution of Eminence Deemed to be University,” is designed to cultivate both practical experimentation with quantum hardware and a robust educational program for future quantum engineers. MAHE’s Vice Chancellor, Dr. Sharath K. Rao, highlighted this commitment, stating, “The MAHE House of Quantum Bengaluru reflects MAHE’s commitment to building advanced scientific capabilities and nurturing talent in emerging technologies.
By creating access to modern quantum infrastructure, we aim to contribute meaningfully to India’s growing quantum ecosystem.” This dual focus differentiates Quantum-Hub@MAHE from facilities primarily dedicated to theoretical research, aligning with the goals of India’s National Quantum Mission to translate scientific advancements into tangible technological capabilities. Faculty and students from both the Bengaluru and Manipal campuses underwent specialized training at Bengaluru and the QuantrolOx laboratory at QuTech, in the Netherlands, preparing them to operate and maintain the advanced quantum infrastructure.

india-deep-tech-380e1ff4d3.headline: Space startup funding hits record $20.8 billion in Q3 as infrastructure investments surge
india-deep-tech-380e1ff4d3.fulltext:
Space startups secured a record $20.8 billion in funding in the third quarter, according to a report by global investment firm Seraphim. The surge came amid heavy investment in launch providers, manufacturing and other infrastructure ventures. The total was nearly triple the $7.4 billion invested in the second quarter and more than double the previous quarterly record.
According to the report, released Wednesday, a record 216 deals were completed during the quarter, up from 140 in the second quarter. Major fundraising rounds included $1.37 billion for Hadrian, $1 billion for Stoke Space and $500 million for K2 Space.
“Capital is following evidence of commercial and institutional demand, not just residual IPO enthusiasm,” said Lucas Bishop, vice president at Seraphim Space.
READ: Indian space tech startup TakeMe2Space to launch AI satellite aboard SpaceX mission (October 1, 2026)
Most of the investment went to infrastructure-related businesses. Companies involved in launch services and broader space access attracted $16.4 billion across 120 deals, while satellite communications, Earth observation and other space-services companies raised $4 billion.
Bishop also noted that defense and sovereign demand are increasingly supporting investment in launch, manufacturing and orbital infrastructure as governments prioritize domestic space capabilities.
However, publicly traded space companies continue to struggle. Bishop said that publicly listed space firms remain loss-making, while SpaceX’s scale and visibility may have drawn investor attention away from smaller publicly traded peers.
North America accounted for about 70% of global funding year to date, while China recorded a quarterly high of $3.3 billion across 49 deals. According to Seraphim, funding is likely to moderate from the third quarter’s exceptional level but remain above historical norms as more companies enter growth and scale-up phases.

Meanwhile, Marlan Space and Loft Orbital announced a $1 billion program to build a 50-satellite, AI-enabled constellation, alongside partners including French AI company Mistral and Amazon.
Earlier, German startup Isar Aerospace became the first commercial European company to put satellites into orbit. The company raised €270 million ($302 million) in June to scale production and expand its launch network. U.S.-based rocket startup Stoke Space also raised $1 billion.

MALTA, N.Y., Oct. 14, 2026 – GlobalFoundries (Nasdaq: GFS) (GF) today announced it has been selected as the technology provider and operator for two new semiconductor manufacturing facilities (“fabs”) at its Malta, New York, site under a U.S.-Japan initiative providing up to $21 billion in funding. Enabled by President Donald J. Trump’s trade and investment agreement with Japan, the initiative will accelerate trusted semiconductor manufacturing in the United States, strengthen critical supply chains and support growing demand across automotive, industrial and connected infrastructure markets.
Japan will provide the investment, while GF will contribute its differentiated technologies, manufacturing expertise and proven operational capabilities as technology provider and operator.
An initial investment of approximately $10 billion will accelerate construction of a new 300mm semiconductor fab, which is expected to come online in 2029. An additional investment of approximately $10 billion would fund a second fab. Together, the two fabs will add significant new U.S. manufacturing capacity and reinforce GF’s ability to support customers worldwide.
“This is a bold new initiative for semiconductor manufacturing, bringing together the United States and Japan with GF’s differentiated technology and decades of manufacturing expertise to accelerate trusted capacity in New York,” said Tim Breen, CEO of GlobalFoundries. “GF was selected because fabs of this scale require more than capital. They require differentiated technology, operational excellence and a proven ability to execute. That combination is what positions GF to make this first-of-its-kind initiative a success.”
The first fab is expected to add approximately 900,000 300mm wafers of annual U.S. manufacturing capacity when fully operational. A second fab would add approximately the same amount. The project is expected to create about 27,000 construction and ecosystem jobs and more than 1,000 high-skilled manufacturing jobs in New York’s Capital Region.
“President Trump’s historic U.S.-Japan Trade Deal is delivering another massive manufacturing investment into America,” said Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick. “With Japan’s investment funding and GlobalFoundries’ partnership, two large semiconductor chip manufacturing facilities will be built in the U.S., creating thousands of high-paying jobs for American workers. This is how the President’s trade agreements result in transformational American industrial assets that strengthen our national and economic security.”
GF has also agreed with the U.S. Department of Commerce to amend its existing CHIPS and Science Act award to reallocate $955 million and accelerate the company’s investments in silicon photonics, silicon-germanium (SiGe) and advanced packaging at its facilities in Malta, New York, and Burlington, Vermont. These investments will expand domestic manufacturing capacity for technologies increasingly critical to communications infrastructure and data centers.
In a separate agreement, the U.S. Department of Commerce will receive equity in GF of approximately four percent, further enabling the American public to share in GF’s growth.
Breaking ground in New York
GF expects to break ground on the first fab at its Malta site later this year. The site is permitted and shovel-ready, using existing Malta infrastructure to speed construction. Details of a groundbreaking event will be announced separately.
Expanding American manufacturing
New York State continues to support the Capital Region’s semiconductor ecosystem through its Green CHIPS program.
“GlobalFoundries’ expansion in Malta is a tremendous vote of confidence in New York’s world-class workforce, innovation ecosystem and the Capital Region’s growing role as a global hub for semiconductor manufacturing and innovation,” said New York Governor Kathy Hochul. “We also look forward to working with the Government of Japan and partnering with their world-leading semiconductor supply chain ecosystem in the years to come. This investment will create thousands of construction jobs, support more than 1,000 highly skilled manufacturing jobs and reinforce New York’s position as a global hub for the semiconductor industry.”
“Since 2009, the people of this site have built one of the nation’s most advanced semiconductor manufacturing operations,” said Grant McEwan, general manager of Fab 8 at GlobalFoundries. “These two great countries entrusting GF to operate two new fabs is a powerful vote of confidence in our workforce, our technology and New York’s Capital Region. With the potential to create thousands of new jobs, we are working with education and workforce partners to build the next generation of semiconductor talent. This is a milestone for our employees, our region and the future of advanced manufacturing in New York.”
Built for customers and partners
The new capacity builds on long-standing customer relationships across the United States and Japan.
“We are planning around GF’s new capacity in New York as an extension of Renesas’ own production footprint, trusted U.S.-based manufacturing backed by a strong U.S.-Japan partnership,” said Hidetoshi Shibata, CEO of Renesas. “This expanded collaboration further strengthens the stable, long-term supply of semiconductors with the differentiated technologies, quality and reliability our products require. These capabilities are essential as we deliver advanced solutions, with demand for electrification, connectivity, AI and data center applications accelerating worldwide.”
“Resilient semiconductor manufacturing depends on a trusted ecosystem of equipment and technology partners,” said Tony Kawai, president & CEO of Tokyo Electron. “Tokyo Electron has supported GlobalFoundries’ manufacturing operations across its global sites for many years, and we are pleased to contribute to expanding advanced semiconductor production capacity in the United States. We also recognize the importance of developing talent and fostering strong local communities to sustain long-term industry growth. This reflects the strong and deeply integrated U.S.-Japan collaboration that underpins the global semiconductor industry.”
“We’ve partnered with GlobalFoundries to produce essential chips for Apple products right here in the United States, as part of our $600 billion commitment to American investment,” said Sabih Khan, Apple’s COO. “As an inaugural member of Apple’s American Manufacturing Program, GlobalFoundries shares our belief in the power of American innovation and ingenuity. This new investment will help accelerate the advanced semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem in the United States.”
“The new fabs in Malta strengthen the U.S. semiconductor ecosystem and give Cirrus Logic access to important domestic manufacturing capability for next-generation mixed-signal products,” said John Forsyth, Cirrus Logic president and CEO. “Building on our long-standing relationship with GF, this new capacity supports the secure, resilient supply chains our customers rely on and broadens the foundation for future innovation.”
“GM is making strategic investments in autonomy and centralized computing to power the next generation of software-defined vehicles and deliver customer-focused technologies at scale, including widespread deployment of AI across our vehicles and breakthrough capabilities like next-generation Super Cruise. This requires significant processing power and a strong, resilient semiconductor supply chain,” said Mark Reuss, president, GM. “GM and GF established the first direct automaker-to-foundry supply agreement, and expanding domestically owned and operated fab capacity in upstate New York marks a decisive step forward for American manufacturing.”

global-economics-694bd0ea66.headline: Fairfax faces CSB conundrum after winning IDBI Bank bid; Merger emerges as likely route
global-economics-694bd0ea66.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-694bd0ea66.fulltext:
While Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd (FFHL)-backed “10955230 Canada Inc.” has emerged as the successful bidder in the strategic restructuring of IDBI Bank, FFHL will now face the challenge of addressing the 40 per cent controlling stake that its step-down subsidiary holds in CSB Bank.
Regulations do not allow a single entity or group to hold controlling stakes in two banks. The options before FFHL, founded by Canada-based Prem Watsa, could therefore be to either merge CSB Bank with IDBI Bank, sell its stake in CSB Bank outright, or seek time from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to pare its holding while relinquishing control of the bank.
FFHL holds a controlling stake in the Thrissur (Kerala)-headquartered CSB Bank through its step-down subsidiary, FIH Mauritius Investments Ltd.
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) on Wednesday approved “10955230 Canada Inc.” as the strategic buyer in the restructuring of IDBI Bank. The transaction, involving the acquisition of a 60.72 per cent stake in IDBI Bank, comprising 30.48 per cent held by the Government of India and 30.24 per cent held by LIC, will be executed for a purchase consideration of ₹52,878 crore.
A merger of CSB Bank and IDBI Bank appears to be the most plausible and synergistic option. While IDBI Bank is a strong, pan-India player in the retail, MSME and corporate banking segments, CSB Bank has carved out strengths in gold loans and Kerala’s NRI banking market.
As of March-end 2026, IDBI Bank’s deposits and advances stood at ₹3,47,163 crore and ₹2,53,626 crore, respectively. In comparison, CSB Bank’s deposits and advances stood at ₹44,246 crore and ₹39,848 crore, respectively. Further, IDBI Bank and CSB Bank had branch networks of 2,174 and 862 outlets, respectively.
IDBI Bank is no stranger to amalgamations. For instance, in 2006, the RBI and the Government amalgamated Satara-based United Western Bank with Industrial Development Bank of India, which had become a banking company in 2004.
While there are likely to be changes at the board level in IDBI Bank, it is unlikely that Fairfax will upset the apple cart by bringing in external executives to manage the bank, given its current operational momentum.
“As for the other two options, an outright sale of the 40 per cent stake in CSB Bank by FFH could attract interest from Axis Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank and YES Bank. Alternatively, if FFH agrees to immediately relinquish control of CSB Bank by withdrawing its directors from the board while seeking time to reduce its shareholding, the RBI may also view this disinvestment route favourably,” said an industry expert.
According to a Finance Ministry statement, the successful bidder will be required to present its credentials to the RBI in line with the Fit and Proper assessment conducted at the Expression of Interest (EoI) stage and submit a roadmap for compliance with the regulatory conditions prescribed therein.
IDBI Bank shares jumped 9 per cent to settle at ₹90.44 on the BSE on Tuesday, while CSB Bank stock rose 4 per cent to close at ₹320.95, as investors cheered the outcome of the IDBI Bank stake sale process.
Once completed, the transaction will mark the largest foreign direct investment (FDI) in India’s financial sector to date.

global-economics-eb48d4a550.fulltext:
ReutersPublished15 Oct 2026, 12:06 AM IST
* Big AI players hit in stock selloff
* Rising rates an increasing concern for some firms
* Investors remain generally sanguine on outlook for sector
By Chuck Mikolajczak, Darshan Kumar R and Shashwat Chauhan
NEW YORK, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Major AI stocks slumped on Wednesday following the latest hot US inflation report, highlighting investor concern about the risks posed by rising borrowing costs in this capital-intensive sector.
Among the leading decliners were data center operator CoreWeave, which fell 16%, AI infrastructure provider Nebius, off 11%, cloud computing giant Oracle, down 9%, and AI server seller Dell Technologies, down 11%. Together the declines erased some $80 billion of market value.
The declines reflect the impact of tightening financial conditions, as well as the outsize gains scored by some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom. Barclays on Wednesday downgraded Dell and two other enterprise hardware stocks, noting that Dell shares have quadrupled this year — part of an AI-fueled investor binge that has resulted in 16 stocks in the S&P 500 technology sector at least doubling this year, according to Reuters calculations.
Concern over rising borrowing costs also weighed on Wednesday's other big decliners. Selling has been particularly intense in CoreWeave, which has issued $22 billion of bonds and $26 billion of loans, according to LSEG data. A CoreWeave bond that was issued in June yielding 9.625% recently yielded 15%.
"We're getting a whole lot of information suggesting that the largest AI companies may not be generating the earnings or revenue people anticipated, and I think that makes everyone nervous about companies like CoreWeave," said Kim Forrest, chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners.
Coreweave Chief Executive Officer Mike Intrator said in an internal memo the market is acting “irrationally” and that he remains confident in the AI cloud company, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday.
Wednesday's rout is the latest sign of a market struggling to come to grips with the implications of high inflation at a time when AI-fueled corporate borrowing has helped push up global interest rates.
Investors generally remain sanguine on the sector in part because its largest players, from chip maker Nvidia to the so-called hyperscalers — primarily Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon — are highly profitable and widely perceived as well managed, despite concerns about debt.
But higher rates will make borrowing and building costlier, a fact that is likely to hit unprofitable and less-profitable firms first. On Wednesday, US interest rates rose following the hot inflation report, pushing the 30-year yield as high as 5.63% before rates pulled back sharply in the afternoon.
"I do think long rates above 5% and creeping towards 6% is a problem for the marginal borrower, I'll call them," said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird, in an interview with Reuters. "It gets a lot harder for the tiers below the kind of big four hyperscalers."
The Nasdaq was down 2% on Wednesday afternoon, with Alphabet and the other major hyperscalers mostly down between around 2%. SpaceX, another major AI player, was down 3%.
"I guess it's grown to a group of five now. SpaceX has kind of joined the party here to join in with like Meta and Microsoft and Google and Amazon," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management. "Those five are spending like 75% of the money that's being invested in data centers here in the country. And those five are obviously putting all their profits and then some into these data centers and the returns they're generating from those are really good."
Despite the strong economics of these firms and their investments, Ellerbroek said it's not surprising that investors remain skeptical about the AI buildout, in part because of the busts that have preceded this one, particularly the dot-com meltdown that started in 2000.
"This select group of companies is driving most of the growth in the economy and the stock market, and they're investing so, so aggressively and investors just aren't really willing to pay for it or fully buy in to the extent that we saw in the late 90s or whatever when investors kind of lost their minds," Ellerbroek said. "Investors have definitely not lost their minds. They're being very cautious and I think selective."
(Reporting by Chuck Mikolajczak and Lewis Krauskopf in New York and Darshan Kumar and Shashwat Chauhan in Bengaluru; editing by Colin Barr and Aurora Ellis)
