Thursday, 15 October 2026
                
Oswal Pumps Limited, one of India's leading manufacturers of solar pumping systems, solar modules and electric motors, today announced that the Board of Directors of its wholly owned subsidiary, Oswal Solar Energy Private Limited ("OSEPL") has approved plans to set up a 1.2 GW solar cell manufacturing facility based on TOPCon (Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact) technology.
The commercial production is expected to commence by April 2028. The entire output is intended for captive consumption by OSEPL's in-house solar module lines. It is intended to secure a steady, reliable supply of DCR cells and reduce the Company's exposure to spot-market price volatility and supplier-driven commercial terms. It will also extend OSEPL's value addition from module assembly into cell manufacturing. Together, these benefits are expected to strengthen the group's cost structure, competitive positioning in Government-backed programmes, and profitability at the consolidated level over time.
The total project cost is estimated at approximately Rs 456 crore. Of this, about Rs 296 crore is proposed to be funded through debt. The balance of Rs 159.85 crore is proposed to be funded from the unutilised IPO proceeds of Rs 163.04 crore, which were originally earmarked for the Aluminium Frame Facility, the remaining 300 MW EVA Encapsulant Facility and the remaining 500 MW Solar Module Facility through infusion in OSEPL. It is proposed to deploy the Net Proceeds towards the aforementioned solar cell manufacturing facility by Financial Year 2028.
The Board of Directors of the Company in its meeting held today, inter-alia, approved variation in the objects/ terms of utilisation of the IPO proceeds and modification of the time limit for the utilisation of the IPO Proceeds, subject to the receipt of requisite statutory/ regulatory approvals including the approval of the Shareholders of the Company.
Strategic rationale
The Company evaluated long-term sourcing arrangements with established domestic cell manufacturers, including multi-year off-take commitments. The commercial terms available, covering both pricing and upfront security deposit requirements, were not aligned with the Company's assessment of long-term value or its approach to prudent working capital management. This puts both availability and cost of the key input outside the Company’s control, a strategic exposure for a business anchored to DCR-dependent programmes (PM-KUSUM, PM Surya Ghar). A comparative evaluation found that setting up captive cell manufacturing capacity was the more economically viable option.
Backward-integrating into cell manufacturing directly addresses this: it secures supply, insulates OSEPL from spot price and deposit demands, deepens value addition from module assembly into cell manufacturing, and is expected to improve the margin and profitability at the consolidated level for the Company.
The change re-directs scarce IPO capital from a low value-add, deferrable component (frames), surplus module capacity, and surplus EVA encapsulant capacity to the highest-leverage point in the chain (cells), where control of supply is now business-critical.
At a capacity of 1.2 GW, it will meet approximately 75% of the OSEPL’s overall cell requirement, with the balance continuing to be sourced externally in the near term.
Commenting on the order, Vivek Gupta, Chairman and Managing Director, Oswal Pumps Limited, said,“The decision to set up a 1.2 GW TOPCon solar cell facility marks a defining step in Oswal Pumps' journey from a pump manufacturer to a fully integrated solar solutions company. Over the years, we have built strong capabilities in solar modules, pumps and complete solar pumping systems. Bringing cell manufacturing in-house completes that value chain and gives us greater control over quality, cost and timelines.
With ALMM List-II now in force, demand for domestically manufactured cells is set to rise sharply. We see this as the right opportunity to invest. Choosing TOPCon technology ensures we are building for the future, with higher efficiency and better long-term performance for our customers.
India's renewable energy ambitions, together with programmes such as PM-KUSUM and PM Surya Ghar, give us strong visibility of demand. We are confident this investment will strengthen our competitive position and create long-term value for all our stakeholders.”

global-economics-259b4b1d24.headline: How Jio got to a $3.2bn IPO in 10 years flat — and what lies next with AI
global-economics-259b4b1d24.fulltext:
Mumbai: When Jio Platforms Ltd announced the price band for its initial public offering on Wednesday, it was an honest nod to equity markets roiled by two wars.
It plans to raise around ₹30,200 crore, or about $3.2 billion, at the upper end of the ₹1,069-1,119 price band announced per share.
The company is seeking an IPO valuation of just over ₹10 trillion, or about $107 billion, lower than its earlier expectations. Even so, Jio’s proposed primary capital raise will rank among its India’s largest IPOs yet alongside automaker Hyundai Motors and others.
Bharti Airtel Ltd, Jio’s closest rival, closed trading on 13 October with a market capitalisation of about ₹11 trillion on NSE. Vodafone Idea Ltd was valued at ₹1.38 trillion. The pricing in the Reliance company's share sale harks back to a decades-old culture of leaving an upside to investors on the table.
Jio Platforms’ valuation pitch rests not only on its core telecom operations but also on a wider range of digital services. The company houses Reliance Industries Ltd’s (RIL) telecom business through its subsidiary Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd, alongside digital applications, enterprise solutions and, more recently, artificial intelligence-backed services.
The telecom business, however, remains central to its valuation. Reliance Jio Infocomm maintains a cozy lead over Airtel as India’s largest telecom operator, with 508.43 million wireless mobile subscribers at the end of August, according to the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai). Separately, it reported a total customer base of 533.3 million at the end of June, including fixed-broadband and business customers.
That said, the wider Reliance group's is betting on artificial intelligence—it is investing heavily in AI infrastructure and large language models (LLMs), which are trained on vast amounts of data to understand and generate human language. LLMs power AI tools such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.
The group is also seeking to build a presence in enterprise AI. In August 2025, Reliance Industries’ billionaire chairman and managing director, Mukesh Ambani, announced the launch of Reliance Intelligence Ltd through a 70:30 joint venture with Meta to develop products for businesses.
In RIL’s latest annual report, Ambani said Reliance Intelligence aims to come up with “sovereign AI capabilities that are designed in India, scaled in India, and made accessible to every Indian—empowering individuals, enterprises, and institutions alike”.
“About 10% of India Inc are firms who are gearing up to be an AI-native organisation and RIL is probably top of the pack,” said an industry executive aware of the AI adoption taking place in the business house that employs more than 400,000 people. For instance, a platform called JioBrain can use AI with 5G and machine-learning tools to spot unusual activity, predict future trends, and automate tasks.
“Then there is also the alliance with Google where every Jio customer has access to Gemini and Gemini Pro. Google pays Jio to bring that product to the customer,” a senior company executive said. (Airtel similarly offers US-based Perplexity AI’s services to its subscribers for a specific period.)
Whether Jio Platforms' initiatives can build a business that its new investors value beyond its telecom operations is a central question for its IPO.
Sounding of the bugle
Mukesh Ambani announced the launch of Jio’s digital services a decade ago, at the company’s 42nd annual general meeting on 1 September 2016. “All voice calls for Jio customers will be absolutely free,” he pronounced. “The era of paying for voice calls is ending.”
In the front row was his son Akash Ambani, then 24, dressed similarly in a black suit, white shirt and red necktie. He was seated between his grandmother, Kokilaben Ambani, the family matriarch, and Manoj Modi, Mukesh’s trusted adviser and friend of more than 40 years.
Mukesh Ambani, then 59, tasked Akash and his twin sister, Isha Ambani—also seated in the front row, dressed in blue—to “acquire 100 million customers on the Jio network in the shortest possible time, and create a new world record”.
That marked the beginning of a decade of upheaval in India’s telecom industry.
The competition failed to anticipate the scale of the disruption that followed when Jio, having skipped the 3G wave entirely, launched its 4G-only services free to subscribers for six months. By the end of that year, just four months later, Jio had 72.16 million mobile subscribers, Trai data show.
Jio bought airwaves in the 800 MHz and 1800 MHz spectrum bands for ₹9,700 crore more than a year before its launch, in March 2015, which helped it build a nationwide network for its 4G services.
Unable to match Jio’s proposition, companies such as Aircel and Reliance Communications Ltd, which was part of Mukesh Ambani’s then estranged brother Anil Ambani’s group, eventually folded.
The industry further consolidated in 2018, when Vodafone India and Idea Cellular merged to form Vodafone Idea Ltd, followed by Airtel’s acquisition of Tata Teleservices Ltd’s consumer mobile business the following year.
But despite the price war triggered by Jio, Airtel has held its ground. Its average revenue per user (Arpu) slipped for the first time in five years to ₹257 per month in the fourth quarter of 2025-26 (January–March 2026) from ₹259 in the preceding three months, but climbed back and ended June 2026 at ₹264. Jio ended the first quarter of FY27 (April–June 2026) with an Arpu of ₹215.6, while Vodafone Idea was at ₹ ₹195.
Both Airtel and Vi, however, trail Jio in subscriber numbers. Airtel had 491.60 million wireless mobile subscribers at the end of August, making it India’s second-largest mobile operator, while Vi had 199.57 million users.
Meanwhile, with an IPO on the horizon, Jio Platforms’ board named Akash Ambani managing director on 9 April, making him the first of Mukesh Ambani’s three children to be appointed to the position.
Telecom 2.0
India’s telecom industry has registered remarkable growth over the past decade, with mobile data consumption increasing nearly 20-fold.
According to Counterpoint Research, low data tariffs, widespread smartphone adoption and a growing ecosystem of digital services transformed consumer behaviour, propelling average monthly data usage from just over 1 GB per person in 2016 to nearly 26 GB in 2026.
“Jio had a role to play in this. It launched not just the network but along with it came a whole gamut of products, including feature phones,” said Tarun Pathak, research director, Counterpoint Research.
The next phase of growth for Reliance Industries hinges on the group’s AI bets, he said, adding that while the previous decade for Jio was about vision and scale, the next will be about expansion and deeper monetisation.
Even after Jio gradually withdrew its free-call offers, its low voice and data tariffs prompted other telecom operators to cut their prices, making mobile services more affordable.
About 267 million handsets were sold in India in 2016, of which 119 million were smartphones, per Counterpoint Research’s data. In 2025, smartphones accounted for about 154 million of the approximately 200 million handsets sold.
The developments had marquee global private equity and strategic investors flocking to India’s telecom sector, particularly Jio.
In 2020 alone, during the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic, Facebook (now Meta), Google, Silver Lake, Vista Equity Partners, General Atlantic, KKR, Mubadala Investment Company, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, TPG, L Catterton, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Intel Capital and Qualcomm Ventures acquired a cumulative equity stake of 32.97% in Jio Platforms for ₹1,52,056 crore. RIL holds a 66.43% stake in Jio Platforms.
These investments, along with a ₹53,124 crore rights issue by Reliance Industries in 2020, helped Jio’s parent company reduce its debt. In June 2020, the oil-to-retail conglomerate declared itself debt-free.
“Jio felt the need to get in some good qualified partners who would add value,” said a senior industry executive aware of the developments at Jio.
Mint interviewed several Reliance, Jio Platforms and industry executives for this report. They declined to be identified as they are not authorised to speak with the media. Spokespersons for Jio Platforms and Reliance Industries did not reply to emails seeking comment.
The making of Jio’s IPO
None of Jio’s investors has opted to sell their stake in the upcoming IPO, which will see the company raising capital through a fresh issue of 270 million equity shares.
In October 2025, Jio had picked Kotak Mahindra Capital Co. and Morgan Stanley India to help prepare for a public market listing through an offer for sale, in which existing shareholders sell their stakes to other investors.
But Jio’s management later decided in favour of an entirely fresh issue of shares as an OFS would have involved multiple rounds of discussions with stakeholders, potentially delaying the IPO, said another person with knowledge of the company’s plans.
“It is not in the company’s DNA to talk to several people and wait for the approvals from various IC (investment committee) of the funds that have invested in Jio Platforms. Hence the decision was made to shift to a purely primary fund raise,” this person said.
According to industry experts, although a large portion of the proceeds from Jio Platforms’ IPO will go towards prepaying Reliance Jio Infocomm’s borrowings, the listing signals the growing importance of the telecom business to Reliance group’s growth.

A KsheerasagarPublished14 Oct 2026, 08:57 PM IST The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) on Wednesday approved the sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax Financial Holdings, founded by Indian-born Canadian billionaire Prem Watsa, for ₹52,877 crore, making it one of the biggest foreign investments in the country’s banking sector. The transaction involves the sale of the government’s 30.48% stake and Life Insurance Corporation of India’s (LIC) 30.24% holding in IDBI Bank. Following the proposed transaction, the government will retain a 15% stake and LIC 19%, taking their combined holding to 34%. Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the strategic partnership would facilitate fresh capital infusion into IDBI Bank and create growth opportunities for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), small industries, and new entrepreneurs. Fairfax has been a major investor in India through Fairfax India Holdings Corporation, which had assets worth $3.8 billion as of June 30, 2026. Its other investments include non-bank lender IIFL Capital and online brokerage firm 5paisa. The proposed transaction comes at a time when the war in the Middle East has strained government finances and weaker foreign inflows have put pressure on the rupee. The IDBI Bank stake sale has long been a target for the government as part of its efforts to reduce state ownership in the banking sector. In October 2022, the government issued a preliminary information memorandum inviting expressions of interest. In July, the government received revised bids from Fairfax and Emirates for the IDBI Bank stake after lowering the reserve price for the sale. Initial bids, invited in the financial year 2025–26, had fallen short of the reserve price and were not approved. With the transaction now cleared by the committee of ministers, following consideration by a panel of senior bureaucrats, it will require regulatory clearances from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). The Fairfax deal is expected to consolidate some of the investor’s existing Indian lending investments in line with regulatory rules. Meanwhile, Fairfax also owns a 40% stake in small private-sector lender CSB Bank Ltd. With Fairfax set to acquire a stake in IDBI Bank, the Canadian investor may be given up to two years to either sell its stake in CSB Bank or merge it with IDBI Bank, as RBI rules prohibit an entity from owning and operating two separate banks, Mint reported in August, citing sources. Gaurav Garg, Head of Research, Lemonn, said this is a fair price for the government, and the bigger win is that a sale first approved in 2021 has finally been done. Fairfax pays ₹81 a share, ₹52,878 crore for 60.72%. That is 6.6% above the ₹75.99 independent fair-value benchmark and covers about two-thirds of the ₹80,000 crore FY27 disinvestment target. The less-noticed point is that the state is not fully leaving. The government and LIC keep 34% between them, with no board seats, and will sell it down over the next few years. Fairfax's real test comes after closing, when it must merge CSB Bank into IDBI within 24 months. The government is handing over control, not walking away; its leftover 34% will shape how this stock trades for years. Gaurav Garg said retail shareholders are holding at a higher price than the new owner paid. IDBI closed at ₹90.39 on 14 October, up about 9% and roughly 12% above Fairfax's ₹81. The compulsory open offer must be priced at ₹81 or the 60-day average market price, whichever is higher. That makes it a safety net, not a payout. Precedent is sobering: when LIC offered ₹61.73 in 2018, only about a fifth of minority holders accepted, and the stock traded below that price four years later. Gains now depend on Fairfax improving the bank, while the government and LIC's 34%, plus Fairfax's eventual cut to 26%, is supply waiting to reach the market. Retail investors are paying more than Fairfax did; the open offer is a floor, not a windfall. The government has approved the strategic restructuring of IDBI Bank, Information Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said.

India's federal government and state-run Life Insurance Corp of India are selling a combined 60.7% stake in IDBI Bank.
